title: the placements: attached, service, batch
intent: The single-threaded objection is real: an agent inside the session of a person blocks that person, and a thread is not the answer, because a thread shares the address space and would take the editor down with it. The references never share an address space with an editor, and that is why they never block one. This wave gives the kernel three placements: attached to a session, in its own Emacs as a service, and in batch; and it opens the second Emacs, using the client-server interface Emacs already has, so that heavy work runs apart and can still act on the buffers of the person.
checks: ./scripts/dev ert tests/unit/test-yeah-state.el tests/unit/test-yeah-loop.el tests/unit/test-yeah-tools.el tests/unit/test-yeah-perm.el tests/unit/test-yeah-session.el tests/unit/test-yeah-compact.el tests/unit/test-yeah-undo.el tests/unit/test-yeah-acp.el tests/unit/test-yeah-emcp.el tests/unit/test-yeah-gptel.el tests/unit/test-yeah-subagent.el tests/unit/test-yeah-shell.el tests/unit/test-yeah-codes.el
objection: Three placements are three chances for the kernel to behave differently, and the differences will be subtle rather than loud: a question answered in one and not in another, an answer whose order depends on the placement.
refuted_by: A run in one placement that produces a different record sequence than the same run in another. If the placement can be observed in the log, the kernel does not know who is driving it.
